--- title: "ASM Chapter 5" author: "Alun ap Rhisiart" date: "10/17/2026" categories: [code, julia, statistics, asm, ecology] execute: echo: true warning: false output: true engine: julia draft: false --- Chapter 5 of Applied Statistical Modelling for Ecologists, by Marc Kéry and Kenneth Kellner, focuses on Ordinary Linear Regression. This chapter also gets in the interesting subject of Post Predictive Checks and Goodness Of Fit. In this chapter, we use a simulated dataset about wallcreepers (which we don't have in the UK, grrrh). I guess this is very familiar to most people. If the value of our dependent variable $y_i$ varies acconding to independent variable $x_i$, then $$\mu = \alpha + \beta\cdot x_i$$ We take this to deterministic, linear part to be the mean, or expected value. $$y_i\sim{Normal(\alpha + \beta\cdot x_i, \sigma^2)}$$ We can also express this as a linear equation for the mean plus an error term. $$y_i = \alpha + \beta\cdot x_i + \epsilon_i$$ $$\epsilon_i\sim{Normal(0, \sigma^2)}$$ So, we have an overall intercept, a coefficient for the effect of x, which will be a regression line, and some scatter around that line which is normally distributed but centered on the line itself. ## 5.2 Data generation As usual, the data is simulated, so we know the real value of the parameters, and can check that our model can recover them. ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Random Random.seed!(5) n = 16 # number of years var = 25 # residual variance truth = (α = 40, β = -0.5, σ = sqrt(var)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (α = 40, β = -0.5, σ = 5.0) ``` ::: ::: Next, we plot the generated data. As in previous chapters, although we can get random numbers from the Normal distribution, they won't exactly match the book output, because it is a different RNG. So we will just drop into R to get the value of epsilon. I fudged putting the sd into R because R doesn't know Unicode; I could just use roman letters (eps) for the variable, but it isn't important here, since I just want to get the same numbers. In reality, I would use the Julia RNG anyway. ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using RCall @rput n R"set.seed(5);eps <- rnorm(n, 0, sd = 5)" @rget eps ``` ::: ::: {#6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using StatsPlots, Distributions ϵ = eps x = 1:n y = truth.α .+ truth.β .* x .+ ϵ scatter(1989 .+ x, y, xlabel="Year", ylabel="Wallcreeper Count", title="Simulated Wallcreeper Data") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## 5.3 Analysis with Canned Functions in Julia This section is going to fit a linear regression model to the simulated wallcreeper data using Julia's built-in functions, and then we will try ot match the output from the R package DHARMa, knowing that if this is difficult we can always drop into R for such things. ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using GLM, StatsBase data = (; x = x, y = y) model = lm(@formula(y ~ x), data) model ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` StatsModels.TableRegressionModel{LinearModel{GLM.LmResp{Vector{Float64}}, GLM.DensePredChol{Float64, LinearAlgebra.CholeskyPivoted{Float64, Matrix{Float64}, Vector{Int64}}}}, Matrix{Float64}} y ~ 1 + x Coefficients: ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Coef. Std. Error t Pr(>|t|) Lower 95% Upper 95% ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── (Intercept) 40.7426 2.40168 16.96 <1e-10 35.5915 45.8937 x -0.690722 0.248376 -2.78 0.0147 -1.22344 -0.158009 ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ``` ::: ::: ### 5.3.2 Goodness-of-fit assessment THe book prints out the residuals, which we can do also, but it also gives the code, but not the plot, of a histogram. I'll display it here, although it isn't that useful for such a small dataset. ::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} histogram(residuals(model), bins = 20, xlabel = "Residuals", ylabel = "Frequency", title = "Histogram of Residuals" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ### 5.3.3 Computing Predictions ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} predictions = predict(model) predictions ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 16-element Vector{Float64}: 40.051873886693 39.36115163107664 38.670429375460266 37.9797071198439 37.28898486422753 36.598262608611165 35.90754035299479 35.21681809737843 34.52609584176206 33.83537358614569 33.14465133052932 32.453929074912956 31.763206819296585 31.072484563680216 30.38176230806385 29.69104005244748 ``` ::: ::: ## 5.4 Bayesian Analysis We will translate the JAGS version of the linear regression model into a Bayesian analysis using Julia's Turing package. Now we start to see some major differences between the way you would approach this is BUGS/JAGS and how you do it in Turing (or more generally using a HMC/NUTS sampler). In the JAGS code, you put everything into the model block, including priors, likelihood, posterior predictive checks, derived residuals, etc. In Turing, this would break the NUTS sampler. In JAGS, the model string is a scripting language telling JAGS what nodes to track during its Gibbs sampling loops. In Turing, the @model macro defines a strict probabilistic log-density target for the sampler. Everything else, residuals, fit statistics, predictive datasets, etc, is just standard Julia code applied to the resuling DataFrame or Chain. Since Julia is fast, we don't have to convert this into a different language such as C++. ::: {.callout-note} The Turing philosophy is: fit the parameters in the model, generate predictions outside the model. ::: ::: {#14 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Turing, FlexiChains, MCMCDiagnosticTools @model function linear_regression(x, y) # Priors. tau = 0.0001 is sd = 100 α ~ Normal(0, 100) β ~ Normal(0, 100) σ ~ Uniform(0, 100) # Likelihood μ = α .+ β .* x y ~ product_distribution(Normal.(μ)) end model = linear_regression(x, y) chains = sample(model, NUTS(), MCMCThreads(), 10000, 4; progress=false) ``` ::: ::: {#16 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} summarystats(chains) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: Alpha and beta are close, sigma is very different. Now we can check for convergence. ::: {#18 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} plot(chains; size=(800,600)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ::: {#20 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} # Extract parameter vectors from the chain alpha_post = vec(Array(chains[:α])) beta_post = vec(Array(chains[:β])) sigma_post = vec(Array(chains[:σ])) S = length(alpha_post) # Number of posterior draws fit = zeros(S) # Sum of squares for actual data fit_new = zeros(S) # Sum of squares for new data # Generate y.new and compute discrepancies for every posterior draw for s in 1:S # 1. Expected values for this iteration μ = alpha_post[s] .+ beta_post[s] .* x # 2. Generate replicate dataset y_new = rand.(Normal.(μ, sigma_post[s])) # 3. Calculate squared residuals fit[s] = sum((y .- μ).^2) fit_new[s] = sum((y_new .- μ).^2) end # Calculate the Bayesian p-value (proportion of times fit_new > fit) bp_val = mean(fit_new .> fit) println("Bayesian p-value: ", round(bp_val, digits=3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Bayesian p-value: 0.956 ``` ::: :::
